title: The Retail Silence That Reshapes The Amazon Stock Bull Case
detail:
The Retail Silence That Reshapes The Amazon Stock Bull Case
Trefis Team
Tue, August 25, 2026 at 9:55 AM MDT 4 min read
AMZN
META
MSFT
NFLX
GOOG
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure
Photo by justynafaliszek on Pixabay

Management's narrative has pivoted hard from optimizing its massive retail machine to funding aggressive AI infrastructure buildouts, quietly changing what an investment in the company is actually a bet on.

For the better part of two years, if you held Amazon (AMZN) stock, you were betting on efficiency. The story management told was about shaving pennies and seconds off the cost of moving a box from a warehouse to your door. Now, that efficiency story shares the stage with a much larger narrative. In its place is a focused narrative backed by hard numbers: management's plan to invest approximately $200 billion in cash capital expenditures in 2026, with the vast majority allocated to support AWS and AI infrastructure. The relative shift in focus matters, because it signals a profound shift in where Amazon's weight now sits, and what you, as a holder, are truly betting on today.

Fulfillment Efficiency Meets the AI Capital Wave

Not long ago, the company's earnings calls positioned retail logistics as the primary headline act. Management consistently highlights how they continue to lower per-unit fulfillment costs—with CFO Brian Olsavsky dedicating prepared remarks to regional inventory placement, consolidation rates, and scaling robotics. Optimizing North America retail remains a foundational engine, generating $426.3 billion annually (59% of revenue).

However, while cost-to-serve improvements remain steady in the background, the headline narrative and capital expenditure focus have decisively expanded toward Amazon Web Services (AWS) and AI infrastructure.

The New $169 Billion Story

The airtime has been seized by Amazon Web Services (AWS) and its all-in bet on artificial intelligence. The new story is one of staggering scale and acceleration. Management now leads with the fact that AWS is a "$169 billion annualized revenue run rate business." They are building a narrative around their custom silicon, now a business with a chips revenue run rate "over $25 billion," and an AI-specific revenue run rate also "over $25 billion." The center of gravity has moved decisively. While the North America retail segment posted steady full-year growth of 10% in FY2025, AWS grew 20% over the same period. That momentum carried directly into 2026, with AWS accelerating for its fifth consecutive quarter to deliver 37% year-over-year revenue growth in Q2. That is where the energy, the capital, and the story now live.

Why the Story Simply Moved On

This shift is reassuring. The moderated emphasis on retail efficiency doesn't appear to be hiding a problem; that segment is still a massive, profitable engine growing at 10%. Instead, the quiet reflects a deliberate choice to focus on a much larger, faster-growing opportunity. More than just another division, AWS's growth is now the primary driver of the entire company's valuation narrative.

title: The Price of Progress for Google Stock
detail:
The Price of Progress for Google Stock
Trefis Team
Tue, August 25, 2026 at 9:44 AM MDT 4 min read

AMZN
MSFT
META
NFLX
Explore stocks on Coinbase

Photo by ArcNovaStudio on Pixabay

If you hold Alphabet (GOOGL) stock, the recent top-line numbers look spectacular. In the second quarter of 2026, the company delivered 24% overall revenue growth, propelled by an 82% surge in its Google Cloud segment. This is the AI-fueled future investors have been waiting for. But beneath the surface of that growth, a fundamental shift is underway in the company's financial DNA, and it represents the most significant risk to the stock today.

The core issue is that the cost of competing in the AI arms race is so immense it's beginning to strain the famously efficient Alphabet financial model. This isn't a story about AI failing; it's a story about the price of ensuring it succeeds.

The AI Arms Race Is Draining the Coffers

"For years, Alphabet has been a reliable cash engine, generating $53.3 billion in free cash flow over the trailing twelve months. However, that run hit an unprecedented speed bump in the second quarter, when massive AI infrastructure spending pushed quarterly free cash flow into negative territory at -$5.9 billion. Management has raised its CapEx guidance to a range of $195 billion to $205 billion. Executives were clear that investors should expect that "free cash flow will remain under pressure."

The mechanism here is straightforward: spending on the technical infrastructure for AI, servers, data centers, networking, is consuming cash faster than the business generates it. This spending is seen as non-negotiable. As one analyst noted, there are concerns Google needs to keep pace with "other leading labs," and management itself stated that it "will need Gemini 4 as a larger base model to compete at that frontier level." If this investment doesn't produce a clear lead in AI, or if the returns prove elusive, investors could begin to question the entire strategy, which would pressure the stock's valuation multiple.

Profit Margins Are Sitting at a Five-Year Peak

Compounding the cash drain is the fact that Alphabet's profitability is currently at a cyclical high, giving it more room to fall than to rise. While Alphabet's headline net margin sits at an anomalous 55%—heavily inflated by non-operating unrealized gains on its equity investments—its core operating margin of 33% is genuinely at the high end of its multi-year range, well above its 3-year average of 31%.

These peak margins are now facing direct pressure from the AI investment cycle. The surge in CapEx leads to higher depreciation costs, which hits the operating margin line directly. Furthermore, management has signaled it will use more expensive third-party capacity to meet demand, warning this "will create modest margin pressure in the near term." A reversion of these historically high margins back toward their long-term average would significantly slow earnings growth, even if revenue continues to climb. At stake is the exceptional profitability that has long justified a premium for the stock.

Coinbase tokenized US equities went live on Base on Monday, putting four technology stocks onchain as transferable tokens that eligible non-US users can hold in a self-custodial wallet with no brokerage account required.

NVDAc, AAPLc, METAc, and GOOGLc track Nvidia, Apple, Meta, and Alphabet, and Chainlink now sits as the official oracle piping price data into roughly 50 Base apps that support the tokens.

The launch matters less for the four tickers than for what runs underneath them. Coinbase is an issuer, chain operator, and one of the trading venues simultaneously, and Chainlink's feed is the piece that determines whether these tokens function as passive holdings or as usable DeFi collateral.

Discover: The Best Crypto to Diversify Your Portfolio

Coinbase Tokenized Stocks, A $2.48 Billion Market Getting Crowded

Tokenized public equities now total $2.49 billion, up 5.18% over 30 days, with 2.12 million holders and $27.28 billion in monthly transfer volume, according to rwa.xyz.

Ondo leads with $872.7 million across 406 assets, followed by Backed's xStocks at $588 million and Binance's bStocks at $552.7 million. Coinbase enters fourth with just four tickers and a promise of more.

Combined onchain value for the four Coinbase tokens sat near $4.55 million late Monday against $3.06 million of DEX liquidity and $10.8 million in 24-hour volume.

Source: RWA.XYZ

NVDAc, the largest, had 6,794.49 tokens outstanding across 1,745 holders, according to BaseScan. Pricing tracked the underlying tightly: NVDAc changed hands at $208.51 against Nvidia's $208.48 close, AAPLc at $311.23 against Apple's $310.34, and METAc at $558.50 against Meta's $559.02.

Aerodrome captured the deepest liquidity for every token, holding $957,307 behind NVDAc and between $619,000 and $669,000 behind the others. AERO itself traded at $0.5334, up 11.3% on the day and 29% over the week on $94.3 million of volume, with the DEX carrying $265.8 million in total value locked against a $522 million market cap.

Base's overall TVL stands at $5.49 billion, fourth among all chains behind Ethereum, BNB Chain and Solana, per DefiLlama, a base of onchain liquidity that networks like Ethereum continue to compete for as RWA infrastructure scales.

Chainlink Feeds and the Weekend Gap

Chainlink's feeds publish total return values that fold in dividend and split adjustments rather than raw equity prices, and they run 24/5, freezing during corporate actions. The tokens themselves trade 24/7, which creates a structural mismatch any integrator has to handle deliberately.

title: AMD Is Winning Nvidia (NVDA) Customers But Investors May Be Missing The Catch
detail:
AMD Is Winning Nvidia (NVDA) Customers But Investors May Be Missing The Catch
Habib Ur Rehman
Mon, August 24, 2026 at 10:33 PM MDT 3 min read
AMD
NVDA
META
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) has finally landed the kind of AI customers investors spent years waiting for. OpenAI and Meta have committed to massive deployments of AMD Instinct GPUs, helping validate the company as the clearest large-scale alternative to Nvidia Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA). But Morgan Stanley thinks one less-discussed part of those deals makes the profit story much uglier than the customer logos suggest.

The issue is the warrants. AMD issued OpenAI and Meta warrants covering up to 160 million shares each at an exercise price of $0.01. Together, that is 320 million potential shares, equal to nearly 20% of AMD's roughly 1.63 billion shares outstanding. AMD's own OpenAI filing described the warrant as a "material inducement" for entering the supply agreement.

AMD Is Winning Nvidia (NVDA) Customers But Investors May Be Missing The Catch

Morgan Stanley analyst Joseph Moore focused on that cost in an August 5 note. He estimates AMD is effectively issuing more than $15 billion of warrants for every $15 billion to $20 billion of revenue tied to OpenAI and Meta. If the economic value of those warrants were treated like a cash expense, Moore argued, the profitability of that GPU business could disappear. He still called the strategy sensible because it can accelerate adoption, but said the warrants put an asterisk next to AMD's AI progress.

That is the contradiction investors have to price. Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMD) reported second-quarter revenue of $11.5 billion, up 50% year over year, while Data Center revenue more than doubled to $6.7 billion. The customer wins may not tell us as much about AMD's organic competitive position as the headlines imply if exceptional equity incentives helped secure them.

There is an important counterpoint. None of the 320 million warrant shares had vested as of June 27. Vesting requires huge GPU purchase milestones and other conditions, while the OpenAI warrant also carries AMD share-price thresholds reaching as high as $600. If those conditions are met, AMD shareholders may be getting huge revenue growth alongside the dilution.

Insider Monkey's database showed 165 hedge funds with long positions in AMD at the end of Q2 2026, up 23% from 134 in Q1. Marshall Wace held about 3.90 million shares after increasing its position 3% during the quarter. Those filings predate Morgan Stanley's August note. Short interest stood at 37.75 million shares on July 31, or about 2.3% of float, with 1.3 days to cover.

At roughly 42 times forward earnings, AMD is already priced for major AI success. The OpenAI and Meta wins strengthen that case, but the economics suggest investors should distinguish market-share gains from profitable market-share gains.

title: Prediction: This Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock Will Be Worth More than SpaceX Before 2026 is Over
detail:
Prediction: This Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stock Will Be Worth More than SpaceX Before 2026 is Over
Keithen Drury, The Motley Fool

Space Exploration Technologies, better known as SpaceX, has seen its valuation fluctuate since going public just over two months ago. Its valuation hit $2.6 trillion just days after going public, but then sold off to a low of $1.4 trillion before rebounding to its current $1.8 trillion level (at the time of this writing). However, I think one stock could be worth more than SpaceX before 2026 is over, and it's currently valued at a lower level than anything SpaceX has traded at during its time on the public markets.

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) is currently a $1.39 trillion company, but I think it could easily surpass SpaceX before 2026 is over for a handful of reasons, not all of them in its control.

Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.
Does SpaceX deserve to be bigger than Meta?

The first question investors need to ask is whether SpaceX logically deserves to be bigger than Meta. I think the answer to that question is a resounding "no."

First, let's look at what each company is doing right now. During Q2 2026, Meta Platforms' revenue totaled $60.8 billion, rising 28% year over year. It had rising expenses, which caused net income to shrink 14% year over year, but it still posted an impressive $15.8 billion profit. Those are figures you'd expect from a company valued at over $1 trillion, but it's nowhere near what SpaceX is producing.

From a growth standpoint, SpaceX is beating Meta, with revenue rising 92% year over year. However, its revenue only totaled $7.8 billion, and it produced no net income to speak of. That's right: SpaceX's revenue is less than half of Meta's net income, yet SpaceX has a higher valuation.

That doesn't make a lot of sense logically, even if SpaceX is growing at a rapid pace. Because of these mismatched figures, I wouldn't be surprised to see Meta end 2026 at a higher valuation than SpaceX, and it could occur in two ways.

Meta is cheap while SpaceX is expensive

By the end of 2026, Meta will be bigger than SpaceX through one of two mechanisms. First, Meta Platforms could rise to have a reasonable valuation. Right now, Meta trades for 17.5 times forward earnings. For reference, the S&P 500 trades for 21.4 times forward earnings.

META PE Ratio (Forward) data by YCharts

That's a very low price, indicating that Meta is trading at the cheaper end of its usual valuation range. Some of its valuation woes are due to lackluster performance, but with Meta still growing rapidly and profits only falling due to the acquisition of major (AI) talent, I think this is just too low a price to pay for Meta's stock.
